final_answer:
>>> When an mRNA vaccine is injected, it enters the body as a small molecule encased in a protective lipid nanoparticle.  
>>> The lipid coating helps the mRNA evade the immune system and deliver it into nearby cells (e.g., muscle or fat cells at the injection site).  
>>> Once inside the cell, the mRNA is released and travels to the ribosomes, which are the cell’s protein-making machinery.  
>>> The ribosomes read the mRNA’s genetic code and produce a viral protein (e.g., the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2).  
>>> The newly made protein is displayed on the cell’s surface, flagging it as foreign to the immune system.  
>>> Dendritic cells (a type of immune cell) detect the protein, process it, and present fragments of it to T-cells and B-cells.  
>>> B-cells produce antibodies specific to the viral protein, while T-cells are activated to destroy infected cells.  
>>> The immune system generates memory B-cells and T-cells, which remain in the body to provide long-term immunity against future infections.  
>>> The mRNA is quickly degraded by the cell, ensuring it does not integrate into the genome or cause lasting changes.  
>>> This process primes the immune system to recognize and neutralize the actual virus if encountered later, without causing disease.
